analysis.one_liner: Requires HHS to publicly list hospitals that violate the hospital price transparency rule.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and received no vote in the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal price transparency rule already requires hospitals to post clear, accessible prices for their items and services online. This bill would force the Department of Health and Human Services to publish a public list of every hospital that got a penalty, warning notice, corrective action request, or any written communication about potential noncompliance, and to disclose those enforcement documents in full without redaction. It would also require annual reports on complaints and enforcement, and a GAO study with recommendations, including whether to strip tax-exempt status from noncompliant hospitals and raise penalty amounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers, and anyone paying hospital bills, who would be able to see which hospitals hide their prices and use posted prices to shop and compare before care.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to maintain a publicly available list on the CMS website of hospitals not in compliance with the price transparency rule, including any hospital that received a civil monetary penalty, a warning notice, a corrective action plan request, or any written communication about potential noncompliance.
Makes any penalty, notice, or enforcement communication subject to full public disclosure under FOIA, without redaction, so hospitals cannot keep enforcement records hidden.
Requires annual public reports on complaints and enforcement, and directs GAO to report on compliance and recommend improvements to price transparency for patients, employers, and the public.

Directs GAO to recommend revoking or suspending the tax-exempt status of noncompliant hospitals and increasing civil monetary penalties, and requires HHS to propose a rule based on those recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Noncompliant hospitals, which would face public exposure of their enforcement records, and potentially larger fines or loss of tax-exempt status if the GAO recommendations are adopted.

drawbacks.text: The bill increases disclosure and reporting but does not itself raise the existing civil monetary penalties (currently capped in the low five figures per hospital per year under existing rules) or directly enforce anything; actual compliance still depends on follow-up rulemaking after the GAO report.

Hospitals argue that publishing compliance communications could be unfair to facilities that are in the process of correcting problems, since any written communication about potential noncompliance would appear publicly even before a violation is confirmed.
Administrative costs fall on HHS and CMS to maintain the list, process disclosures, and produce annual reports, though these are modest for a federal agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is small: maintaining a public list and writing reports. The benefit depends on follow-through, since the bill's teeth (bigger fines and possible loss of tax-exempt status) only take effect if HHS proposes a rule after the GAO report. Still, sunshine on which hospitals hide their prices is a low-cost, meaningful step for patients trying to compare prices in one of the most opaque corners of the economy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 15, 2023, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill in the Senate on November 15, 2023, for himself and Senator Budd.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken; the bill sat in committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and it never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Noncompliant hospitals avoid public listing and potential penalties, and patients remain without a public enforcement record of which hospitals hide prices.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to force HHS to publish a list of hospitals violating the price transparency rule.

for.name: Sen. Ted Budd
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, but no committee or floor vote was ever held, so the broader partisan split was never tested; price transparency has generally drawn bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill would publicly name hospitals that fail to post their prices, expose their enforcement communications without redaction, and set in motion recommendations for larger fines and possible loss of tax-exempt status. Hospital hiding of prices keeps patients from comparing costs and contributes to surprise billing; the bill's value runs directly against hospitals' interest in keeping negotiated rates out of sight.

The bill explicitly aims to improve transparency to employers, who pay hospital bills through their plans and lack the market information hospitals currently withhold. Better price data helps them negotiate and design cheaper plans.
